message.reasoning:
I need to decide whether to sell houses or declare bankruptcy for a $50 rent payment.

Selling one orange house returns $50, covering the $27 shortfall. I must check the building evenness rule.

The building evenness rule allows selling one house from one property while keeping the others at four. The bank has no houses remaining.

Releasing one house returns it to the bank. Opponents could then build on their red properties. I am checking whether p2 can even out their red houses with just one house.

I am calculating the rent values for the red properties to assess the risk of releasing one orange house. Kentucky Avenue with four houses would charge $875, while Indiana Avenue with three houses would charge $700.

I checked the remaining red and yellow properties. Opponents could buy the released house, but bankruptcy would lose my orange monopoly entirely. I will sell one house for $50.

All three orange properties lose $200 in rent when one house is removed. No property is more strategic to sell from than the others.

St. James Place is the least landed orange property, while New York Avenue is hit most often. I will sell one house from St. James Place to preserve New York and Tennessee at four houses.

I am now checking whether p2 or p4 can actually afford to buy the released house. p2 has $45 cash, which is too little to build on Kentucky Avenue. p4 has $216 and could purchase a house for $150, but they would still need to even out their yellow properties.

Only p4 can afford the released house. They would raise one yellow property from two to three houses, increasing rent from $390 to $900. This is a notable risk, but bankruptcy is the only alternative.
